description: We are Analytica, a student-led data and AI competition league from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), structured as an academic extension project. Our members compete in hackathons and data science challenges throughout the year, run internal training, and partner with companies on applied analytics projects. Our stack is mostly Python for data and ML, TypeScript with React for the frontend. Core strengths: data engineering, machine learning, statistics, and LLM applications.
summary:
HabitatFire is a web platform that turns NASA microgravity combustion data into design tools for lunar habitats and spacecraft. Decades of fire experiments are scattered across thousands of records, videos and reports, which makes them hard for habitat designers to use.

It has three tools, all built on one shared index of the data:
(1) SI, an AI research assistant. It understands what the user is asking, cross-references NASA PSI records and technical documents, ranks the relevant investigations and cites every source.
(2) Semantic search. Every experiment is indexed by material and test conditions, so users can find experiments by details their titles never mention.
(3) A fire-spread simulator. A stochastic model fitted to NASA SAFFIRE flight images predicts how fire spreads across fabric items inside a lunar habitat or a spacecraft in lunar orbit. Users place items, choose where the fire starts, and compare layouts.

Results can be exported as model-ready CSV or JSON, with units and data sources.

It addresses the challenge by bringing fire evidence gathered over decades in orbit into Artemis-era design. As crews stay longer on and around the Moon, fire stays one of the most severe hazards, and HabitatFire helps teams design safer lunar homes before the first spark.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

HabitatFire is a web platform that makes NASA's microgravity combustion research usable for designing lunar habitats and spacecraft. It has three connected tools.

1. SI, the research assistant

Users ask questions in plain language, for example "Which experiments should I use to analyze flame spread over cabin fabrics at elevated oxygen?". SI understands what is being asked, searches NASA PSI records and technical documents, ranks the most relevant investigations and writes an answer with numbered citations. Before the answer is shown, every citation and number is checked against the evidence SI actually retrieved, and an audit line reports the result. Selected data can be exported as CSV or JSON, with units and provenance.

2. Semantic search

Each of the 24 combustion investigations is indexed by meaning: its materials, test conditions and findings. A search for "cotton-fiberglass fabric" finds the SAFFIRE experiments, even though their titles never use those words. Results highlight the matching passage and are labeled when they were found by meaning rather than by title.

3. Fire-spread simulator

An interactive 3D model of a lunar surface habitat or a spacecraft in lunar orbit. Users choose the atmosphere from NASA's exploration presets (for example 34% O₂ at 56.5 kPa for the lunar surface), place and size fabric items (curtains, liners, partitions, bags), and click to start the fire. The simulator runs 20 realizations and reports area burned, flame-front speed and which items catch fire. Users can save layouts and compare them on the same random seeds.

HOW THE SIMULATION WORKS

It is a stochastic cellular model on the experiment's own grid: 10×20 mm cells and 2-second steps. Each cell ignites with a probability that depends on its burning neighbors, and those probabilities were fitted to SAFFIRE flight images of burning fabric. Fire passes from one item to another only where they touch, so a gap between items acts as a firebreak. The simulator uses the SAFFIRE trial whose oxygen, pressure and airflow are closest to the chosen atmosphere. A "Where this comes from" panel shows the source trial, its flight imagery and the parameters derived from it.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite; 3D scenes with Three.js (react-three-fiber).

- Backend: Python, with answers streamed live to the browser as the assistant writes them.

- AI: Claude (Anthropic) with our own tools for searching, ranking investigations and querying PSI records.

- Retrieval: keyword search (BM25) combined with Voyage AI embeddings stored in MongoDB Atlas.

- Hosting: AWS EC2, with the public site at habitatfire.us.

- Data: NASA PSI (24 investigations, 2,001 records, 1,629 videos), SAFFIRE I–VI, BASS-II, SAME, SoFIE-GEL, NASA reports (FM², the Mir and Apollo fire reports, the PSI Researcher's Guide) and published JAXA FLARE results.

- Quality: 65 automated tests for the simulation and data pipeline, plus backend tests.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Fire is one of the most severe hazards for crewed missions: there is nowhere to evacuate to, and in microgravity flames behave differently than on Earth. NASA has collected decades of evidence, but it is spread across thousands of records and videos. HabitatFire gives designers, students and researchers one place where they can go from a question to the evidence, from the evidence to the data, and from the data to a scenario they can test. Teams can compare cabin layouts and atmosphere choices early in design, when changes are still cheap, in support of Artemis-era habitats and vehicles.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a static database browser, HabitatFire links the evidence directly to a simulation whose parameters come from real flight imagery. A user can go from "what does NASA know?" to "what would happen in my cabin?" in a few clicks, and every number can be traced back to the experiment it came from.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific traceability: every answer cites its sources, and every simulation parameter links back to the SAFFIRE trial it came from.

- Clear scope: the spread model is fitted to the fabric SAFFIRE tested in flight (cotton-fiberglass, SIBAL). The other experiments are shown as flight replays and evidence, not as models of their own, and we say so in the model details.

- Usability for non-specialists: plain-language questions, sensible default scenarios and the technical details one click away.

- Openness and growth: the same pipeline can take in new data, such as NASA's planned FM² lunar flammability results, and add materials as new microgravity tests are published.
